summary: Waiting to learn whether this repository is public or private
detail: sensei has not yet captured the forge’s answer for this repository, so it cannot tell who decides whether it is shared. Until then it is not shared, deliberately: treating it as public would hand the choice to you when it may be your organisation’s, and treating it as private would make it org-mandated when it may be yours.

summary: The forge’s answer for this repository is out of date
detail: A repository that turns private upstream must stop being treated as public — otherwise it would keep syncing free, under an authority that no longer applies. An old capture is therefore treated as no capture.

summary: This organisation has not been claimed
detail: Nobody has proven ownership of this organisation in the dōjō yet, so it cannot hold a subscription and its private repositories cannot be shared.
remedy: Ask an owner of the organisation to claim it

summary: No active subscription for this organisation
detail: Private repositories are subscription-gated whoever owns them. Public repositories are free and unaffected.

summary: The subscription has lapsed
detail: The organisation had a subscription and its billing period has ended, so private repositories stopped syncing.

summary: You have not turned sharing on for this repository
detail: This repository is yours to decide — it is either personal or public — so nothing is shared until you say so.
remedy: Turn sharing on for this repository

summary: Your organisation has not enabled sharing for its private repositories
detail: This repository is private and owned by an organisation, so the organisation decides. Your own preference does not apply to it, in either direction.
remedy: Ask an admin to enable sharing

summary: This metric is not in service yet
detail: The catalogue gives it a start date later than today. It is not broken and there is nothing to fix; it will begin computing on its own.

summary: This metric has been retired
detail: Past its end date in the catalogue. Rows it already wrote are kept on purpose — retirement is in place, never a hand-deletion — so historical readings stay explicable. Nothing new is computed.

summary: Every dojo sharing this repository switched this metric off
detail: A deliberate choice, not a fault, and it is why nothing is being computed. Deactivation is per (dojo, repository, metric): while ANY dojo sharing this repository still wants the metric, it keeps computing. This state means all of them turned it off.
remedy: Turn it back on for at least one dojo

summary: This metric has never run for this repository
detail: No coverage cursor exists yet. Usual for a repository added recently, or one whose group has not had a first successful pass. It is not evidence of failure on its own.

summary: Computed, but this group keeps no day cursor
detail: This metric has produced values for this repository, but its group has no watermark row, so there is no settled-through day to report. The usual reason is cadence: a snapshot group (cost, coverage, knowledge) computes current state only and writes no cursor by design. The same state is also reachable if a day-keyed group wrote values and then failed before sealing, which would show as a repeatedly re-run history.

summary: Up to the last commit this metric walked
detail: A commit-cadence metric (churn, quality) processes only commits newer than the one it recorded. So an absence of recent rows usually means an absence of recent COMMITS, not a stall. Whether newer commits exist is a git fact the database cannot see: compare last_sha against the repository's head.

summary: Calendar days are settled through yesterday
detail: A day-cadence metric settles whole days. Today is never sealed — it reopens as late sessions land — so being settled through yesterday is the current state, not a lag.

summary: Calendar days are unsettled further back than yesterday
detail: A day-cadence metric whose coverage stops before yesterday has real work outstanding. The engine holds a group's cursor when that group fails, so a failing group retries the same range rather than skipping it — which is why a persistent gap here points at a failing group, not at lost days.
remedy: Check the metrics task for a failing group

summary: The ladder reached no verdict for this use site
detail: Every use site is supposed to leave the resolver either placed or carrying a named reason. This one carries neither, which means a rung returned without answering. Treat any blast radius containing it as incomplete by an unknown amount — unlike the other reasons here, this one cannot tell you how much it is hiding.
remedy: Report it: a use site with no verdict is an indexer defect, not a property of your code

summary: The walk saw a syntax shape it does not read yet
detail: The reader recognised that something is used here but not what kind of use it is, so no target could be looked up. This is a gap in the language reader rather than anything about the code — the same expression written a more common way would resolve.
remedy: Check this call site by hand; the graph cannot see through this construct

summary: The type of the thing being called on is not known here
detail: A member call is only placeable once the receiver's type is known, and nothing in this file states it — the value came from a call whose return type is declared elsewhere, from an untyped parameter, or from a binding the reader could not follow. Any first-party member of the same name could be the real target, so the call is reported as doubt rather than guessed at.
remedy: Annotate the receiver, or check members of this name by hand

summary: The declaration states no type to resolve against
detail: The language allows the type to be left out here and it was, so there is nothing written down for the resolver to follow. Distinct from an unknown receiver: nothing was lost in inference, because nothing was ever stated.
remedy: Add an explicit type if this edge matters to you

summary: The name is used here but nothing in scope brings it in
detail: The name resolves to no import, no local declaration and no path this file can see. Most often it is a local variable or a standard-library member that happens to share its name with something declared elsewhere in the project — so a match on name alone would be a wrong edge, not a found one.
remedy: Confirm by hand whether this names the symbol you have in mind

summary: Several declarations match and nothing distinguishes them
detail: More than one declaration in scope answers to this name, and the use site carries nothing that picks one. Emitting the closest or the first would be a coin toss recorded as a fact, so no edge is emitted at all.
remedy: Qualify the reference, or name the file you mean when you ask

summary: The target would only exist after macro expansion
detail: What is called here is produced by a macro, and expansions are not parsed. There is no declaration in the source to point at, so this is a permanent limit of reading source rather than a miss that better inference would close.

summary: The target is chosen at run time, so no static answer exists
detail: The call goes through a trait object, an interface, a function value or a computed key. Which implementation runs depends on data, and reading the source cannot narrow it to one. Reported so a reader knows the path continues somewhere rather than ends here.

summary: Deliberately filtered plumbing, not a failed lookup
detail: Calls like clone, unwrap and toString are filtered on purpose: they are ubiquitous, they are almost never the edge anyone is looking for, and tracking them would bury real dependencies. Its own code so it can be excluded without also excluding genuine misses.

summary: This is where the indexed world ends
detail: Nothing indexed here declares this name, so the target belongs to a library. Named and never opened, by design — the graph maps what you own and the boundary to what you do not. Not a gap: no amount of further inference makes a third-party method a first-party edge.

summary: The file declares the target itself
detail: The use site and the declaration are in one file and the walk read both. Nothing is inferred and there is nothing to be wrong about — the strongest claim the ladder makes.

summary: An import in scope names the path
detail: The source wrote the name down in an import, and the specifier says which module it comes from. That is the segment boundary an identity needs, so nothing about the target is guessed from the shape of the name.

summary: A type in this scan declares the target as its member
detail: The walk read the receiver's type, the barrier type table said where that type lives, and some file in this scan was read declaring exactly that member on exactly that type. The two sides of the merge contract met; nothing here is inferred from the shape of a name. Restricted to members a type OWNS, because a bare name is minted at the use site's own module and matching one across files says only that two files claimed one module path.

summary: A trait impl on the receiver's type supplies the target
detail: A member declared inside `impl Trait for Type` carries the trait as a segment of its identity, so that `Display::fmt` and `Debug::fmt` on one type stay two symbols. A use site writing `w.fmt()` knows the type and the member and cannot know the trait, so the spelling it mints and the spelling the declaration minted can never be the same string. This rung looks the minted spelling up and answers with the declaration's own identity, which the scan produced and this side never assembled. Exactly one declaration must answer to it: two make it ambiguous and place nothing. Weaker than declared_by_its_type, which matched a whole identity, and below it for the same reason the language puts inherent methods first.

summary: A glob in scope covers the module the target sits in
detail: Bound by `use x::*` or equivalent. The ladder knows the glob covers a module that declares this name, but the source never wrote the name down — so this is the weakest first-party rung, and the one to suspect first when an edge points somewhere surprising.

summary: A path rooted in this package, needing no import
detail: The use site spelled a path from the package root, so the path itself carries the module. No import is involved and none is needed.

summary: A fully-qualified path leaving the indexed source
detail: The path names a package the scan does not own, so the target is a library member: named from the path, never resolved by opening the dependency (R5).

summary: A name the language puts in scope everywhere
detail: No import brings it in because the language does not require one. Outranked by a glob — a glob over the same name leaves two possible origins and nothing to tell them apart, and the ladder reports that as ambiguous rather than picking the prelude.
